prompt: A colleague copies a `.class` file compiled on a Mac onto a Linux server with the same Java release. What happens when the server runs it?
hint: What does `javac` write, and for which machine?

choices.text: It fails, because the bytecode holds the Mac processor's instructions
choices.why: Bytecode holds no processor's instructions; it is for the JVM, which is what differs between machines.

choices.text: It runs, because the class file is for the JVM and the server has one
choices.why: Right: the same class file runs on any JVM of that release or later.

choices.text: It runs only after `javac` is run again on the server
choices.why: Recompiling is needed when the release is older, not when the operating system differs.

choices.text: It runs in the interpreter only, since the JIT needs the original machine
choices.why: The JIT compiles for whichever processor the JVM is running on, at run time.

prompt: Java 21's class files carry major version 65. Which major version does a class compiled with `--release 11` carry?
hint: The major version moves by one per release.

prompt: On an Ubuntu 24.04 machine set up as the course does, a build tool reports Java 21 although `java -version` says 25. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which variable does such a tool read before `/usr/bin/java`?

choices.text: `update-alternatives` switched back to 21 after Maven was installed
choices.why: Then `java -version` would say 21 as well; it said 25.

choices.text: The JDK 25 package lacks a compiler, so the tool fell back to 21
choices.why: `openjdk-25-jdk` carries `javac`; and 21 here is a runtime with no compiler at all.

choices.text: `JAVA_HOME` is set to `/usr/lib/jvm/default-java`, which points at 21
choices.why: Right: `default-java` is the archive's default, 21, and tools such as Maven prefer `JAVA_HOME`.

choices.text: The project's class files were compiled with `--release 21`
choices.why: `--release` changes what is written, not which Java the tool runs on.

prompt: Classes were compiled with `javac -d build Report.java`. Which command runs `Report` from the source directory?
hint: `java` needs to be told where the classes are, and then a class name.

choices.text: `java build/Report.class`
choices.why: `java` takes a class name, not a file path; it would look for a class called `build/Report.class`.

choices.text: `java -cp build Report`
choices.why: Right: the class path names the directory, and `Report` is the class to start.

choices.text: `java Report`, because `-d` remembers where it wrote the classes
choices.why: Nothing is remembered; without `-cp` the class path is the current directory, where there is no `Report.class`.

choices.text: `java -d build Report`
choices.why: `-d` is the compiler's option for where to write; `java` uses `-cp` to say where to read.

prompt: A script runs a Java program and checks `$?` afterwards. The program found nothing to do and called `System.exit(0)`. What does the script see?
hint: Which number means success, by convention?

choices.text: 1, because the program stopped early
choices.why: Stopping early is not failing; the status is the number passed to `exit`.

choices.text: Nothing: `$?` is only set when a program throws an exception
choices.why: `$?` holds the status of every command that finishes, Java or not.

choices.text: 0, which the script reads as success
choices.why: Right: the number given to `System.exit` is the status, and 0 means success.

prompt: A job runs `java Report.java` a thousand times a day, and each run takes about a second where a compiled class took a fifth of one. Where does the difference go?
hint: What does source-file mode do before it runs anything?

choices.text: Into starting the compiler and compiling the file in memory, on every run
choices.why: Right: nothing is written to disk, so every run pays for the compiler again.

choices.text: Into the program itself, which runs more slowly when started from source
choices.why: Once compiled, the bytecode is the same; the program runs at the same speed.

choices.text: Into the JIT, which is switched off in source-file mode
choices.why: The JIT works the same way; the extra time is spent before `main` starts.

choices.text: Into writing `Report.class` to disk before running it
choices.why: Source-file mode writes nothing: `ls` showed no class file afterwards.

prompt: Following Java's conventions, which of these names is a constant?

choices.why: camelCase marks a method, a variable or a parameter.

choices.text: `MaxLoans`
choices.why: PascalCase marks a type: a class, interface, enum or record.

choices.text: `maxloans`
choices.why: All lower case, run together, is how a package is named.

choices.text: `MAX_LOANS`
choices.why: Right: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is for `static final` constants.

prompt: `Catalogue.java` declares `public class Inventory`. What happens at `javac Catalogue.java`?

choices.text: It compiles and writes `Catalogue.class`

choices.text: It refuses: a public class must be in a file named after it

choices.text: It compiles, with a warning that the file name breaks the naming convention for classes

prompt: A counter of page views is declared `int` and has reached 2,147,483,647. What does the next `views++` leave in it?
hint: An `int` has 32 bits, and nothing checks the arithmetic.

choices.text: 2,147,483,648, because Java widens it to `long` when needed
choices.why: Java never changes a variable's type; the sum is computed and stored as an `int`.

choices.text: An `ArithmeticException`, thrown by the increment
choices.why: Plain arithmetic on `int` never throws; only methods such as `Math.addExact` do.

choices.text: -2,147,483,648, the smallest `int`
choices.why: Right: it wraps round silently, which is why a count that can pass two billion is a `long`.

choices.text: It stays at 2,147,483,647, the largest value
choices.why: Stopping at the largest value is what a cast from a huge `double` does; `int` arithmetic wraps.

prompt: Two `Integer` variables hold the member ids 4021 and 4021, read from two different files. A test with ids under 100 passed. Why does `if (idA == idB)` now take the wrong branch?
hint: What does `==` compare when both sides are objects?

choices.text: Because `==` on `Integer` compares the values only up to 1000
choices.why: There is no such limit; `==` on objects compares references at every value.

choices.text: `==` compares references, and only values from -128 to 127 share a cached object
choices.why: Right: small values happened to be the same object, which hid the bug; `equals` compares the values.

choices.text: Because reading from a file adds an invisible character to each id
choices.why: The values are equal; `idA.equals(idB)` would say `true`.

choices.text: Because large `Integer` values are unboxed to `long`, which `==` refuses
choices.why: No unboxing happens when both sides are `Integer`; that is the whole problem.

prompt: `var pages = 256;` declares a variable of type `___`, and nothing assigned to it later can change that.
hint: A whole-number literal with no suffix.

prompt: A method declares `double total;` and assigns it inside an `if` and inside its `else`, then prints it. Does it compile?
hint: The compiler checks paths, not values.

choices.text: Yes: every path to the print assigns `total` first
choices.why: Right: definite assignment holds on both branches, so the read is allowed.

choices.text: No: a local must be given a value where it is declared
choices.why: Assigning later is fine, as long as every path does it before the read.

choices.text: Yes, and it would also compile with the `else` removed, since `total` defaults to 0.0
choices.why: Locals get no default; without the `else` there is a path that reads it unassigned, and that is an error.

prompt: A recursive method fails with `StackOverflowError` after about 23,000 calls. A colleague raises `-Xss` to 4m and it reaches about 100,000. What does that fix?
hint: What does `-Xss` size, and what does an endless chain of calls need?

choices.text: Everything: a bigger heap gives the objects in each frame more room
choices.why: `-Xss` sizes each thread's stack, not the heap; and objects live on the heap anyway.

choices.text: Nothing, if the recursion never ends; it only moves where it fails
choices.why: Right: a chain that never returns fills any stack, and a bigger one only delays the error.

choices.text: The cause, because the default stack is too small for any recursion
choices.why: Recursion that ends fits the default stack easily; the default reached 23,254 frames.

prompt: Which of these assignments compiles without a cast?
hint: Java converts by itself only in the direction that cannot overflow.

choices.why: `double` to `int` narrows, and the compiler refuses it even though 3.0 fits.

choices.text: `byte b = someInt;`
choices.why: `int` to `byte` narrows; it needs `(byte)`.

choices.text: `long total = someInt;`
choices.why: Right: `int` to `long` widens, and every `int` fits.

choices.text: `boolean ok = 1;`
choices.why: `boolean` converts to nothing and nothing converts to it; `1` is not `true` in Java.

prompt: A loop does `short stock = 0;` and then `stock += 40_000;` once. It compiles. What is wrong?
hint: What does a compound operator add that `stock = stock + 40_000` would not?

choices.text: Nothing: `+=` checks the range and would have refused a value that does not fit
choices.why: No check happens; the compound operator's hidden cast keeps the low bits silently.

choices.text: It throws `ArithmeticException` at run time, because 40,000 does not fit in a `short`
choices.why: Casts never throw; the result is a wrong number, not an exception.

choices.text: `+=` hides a cast back to `short`, so 40,000 is stored as a negative number
choices.why: Right: 40,000 is above 32,767, and the hidden cast keeps the low 16 bits: -25,536.

prompt: What does `(byte) 300` evaluate to? A `byte` holds -128 to 127, and a narrowing cast keeps the low bits.
hint: Subtract 256 until the number fits.

prompt: `String code = " ab-12 "; code.strip(); code.toUpperCase();` and then `System.out.println("[" + code + "]")`. What is printed?
hint: Where did the results of the two calls go?

choices.why: That would need `code = code.strip().toUpperCase();`: both results were thrown away.
Right: a `String` never changes, and each call returned a new string nobody kept.
`toUpperCase` did not change `code` either; neither call did.
`strip` returned a new string as well, and it was not assigned.

prompt: A program reads a member's name from a file into `name` and tests `name == "Ana"`. The file says Ana. Why can the test be `false`?
hint: Where does a string built while the program runs live?

choices.text: Because `==` on strings is case-sensitive and the file may differ in case
choices.why: The case matches here; `equals` is case-sensitive too and would say `true`.

choices.text: Because strings read from files are stored in another encoding
choices.why: Encoding decides the characters, and these are the same three characters.

choices.text: `==` compares references, and a string read at run time is a new object
choices.why: Right: only literals share one object; `name.equals("Ana")` compares the characters.

prompt: To build a long string in a loop without copying everything so far on every turn, append to a `___` and call `toString()` once at the end.
hint: A mutable buffer of characters.

prompt: A shop's checkout adds prices held in `double`s and compares the total with `==` against the amount the customer was quoted. Sometimes equal amounts compare unequal. What is the sound fix?
hint: Money wants exact decimal arithmetic.

choices.text: Round both sides with `Math.round` before comparing
choices.why: `Math.round` gives whole units, so two prices that differ by cents would compare equal.

choices.text: Hold amounts as `long` cents, or as `BigDecimal` built from strings
choices.why: Right: both are exact, and the comparison then means what it says.

choices.text: Use `float` instead of `double`, which has fewer digits to disagree on
choices.why: `float` has the same binary fractions with fewer bits; it disagrees sooner, not later.

choices.text: Build each `BigDecimal` from the `double` price, `new BigDecimal(price)`
choices.why: That records the `double`'s binary error exactly, all 55 digits of it.

prompt: What does `Math.floorMod(-7, 3)` return?
hint: `floorDiv(-7, 3)` rounds -2.33 down, to -3.

prompt: Which of these evaluate to `true`? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: The sum is 0.30000000000000004 and the literal sits a hair below three tenths.

choices.text: `Double.isNaN(0.0 / 0)`

Yes: the two zeros compare equal, although `1 / -0.0` gives `-Infinity`.

prompt: `int[] backup = shelf;` is meant to keep a copy before `shelf` is sorted. After `Arrays.sort(shelf)`, what does `backup` hold?

prompt: A method receives `int[] prices` and must add 10 to every price in the array. Which loop does the job?
hint: The loop variable of a for-each holds what, exactly?

choices.text: `for (int p : prices) { p = p + 10; }`
choices.why: It compiles and changes nothing: `p` is a copy of each element, and the array keeps its old values.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i < prices.length; i++) { prices[i] += 10; }`
choices.why: Right: writing back needs the position, and the counting `for` is the loop that has it.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i <= prices.length; i++) { prices[i] += 10; }`
choices.why: `<=` runs one pass too many and reads one place past the end, which throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

choices.text: `do { prices[0] += 10; } while (false);`
choices.why: That runs once and touches only the first element.

prompt: `for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { body(); }` runs to the end. Put the first five things it does in the order they happen.

prompt: `Book a = new Book(); Book b = a; b.title = "X";` What does `a.title` hold afterwards?

choices.text: `null`, because only `b` was given a title
choices.why: `b` and `a` lead to one object, so a title set through either is the object's title.

choices.text: Whatever `a` had before, since `b = a` copied the book

Right: one `new`, one object, two references to it.

prompt: On the course's JVM a `Book[1000]` took 4,016 bytes: a 16-byte header and one 4-byte reference per slot. How many bytes does a `Book[500]` take?

prompt: A `NullPointerException` says `Cannot read field "title" because "<local3>" is null`. Why a number instead of the variable's name, and how do you get the name?
hint: What does `javac` keep in a class file by default?

choices.text: Locals were compiled without names; `javac -g` keeps them
choices.why: Right: without that information the JVM has only numbers for the locals, and Maven compiles with it by default.

choices.text: The variable was declared with `var`, which has no name at run time
choices.why: `var` changes nothing in the class file; the numbering comes from the missing debug information.

choices.text: The object was already collected; run with a larger heap
choices.why: A `null` reference never led to an object, so there was nothing to collect.

choices.text: The JVM hides names for security; there is no way to see them

prompt: A class has a field `int loans;` and a method with a local variable `int loans;`. Neither is assigned before being read. What happens?
hint: One of the two is checked by the compiler.

choices.text: Both read 0, because every `int` starts at zero
choices.why: Only the field does; a local has no default at all.

choices.text: Both fail to compile, because neither was initialised
choices.why: A field always has a value, so reading it compiles; the JVM zeroes every new object.

choices.text: Reading the field gives 0; reading the local does not compile
choices.why: Right: the compiler can check one method's paths, and not every place that sets a field.

prompt: A constructor's parameter is called `title`, like the field. To store the parameter in the field, the constructor writes `___.title = title;`.

prompt: A team adds `Book(String isbn, String title)` to a class that had no constructor. Code elsewhere that says `new Book()` now fails to compile. Why?
hint: Where did `Book()` come from before?

choices.text: Two constructors may not exist in one class
choices.why: A class may have as many as it likes, as long as their parameter lists differ.

choices.text: The new constructor must call `this()` on its first line
choices.why: `this(...)` is optional and calls another constructor of the same class; nothing requires it.

choices.text: Fields declared without an initialiser now make `new Book()` illegal
choices.why: Fields keep their defaults whatever constructors exist; the missing piece is the constructor itself.

choices.text: `Book()` is added only when no constructor is declared
choices.why: Right: declaring one removed the free one, and the error lists the constructors that remain.

prompt: A field is declared with no access modifier in class `lib.Shelf`. Which class can read it?

choices.text: `lib.Inside`, another class in the package `lib`

prompt: `Limits.MAX_LOANS` is `static final int` and was changed from 3 to 5. Only `Limits.java` was recompiled, and `Report`, which prints the limit, still prints 3. What does that tell you?
hint: Look at what `javap -c Report` would show where the limit is used.

choices.text: The JVM cached the old `Limits.class` from the previous run
choices.why: Each run loads the class files from disk afresh; `Report` simply never asks `Limits` for the value.

choices.text: `final` fields can only be changed by restarting the machine
choices.why: Nothing about the machine is involved; recompiling `Report` gives 5.

choices.text: The constant 3 was copied into `Report`'s class file when it was compiled

choices.text: A `static` field is read through an object, and no `Limits` object was made

prompt: Inside `public static void main`, the call `greet();` fails with `non-static method greet() cannot be referenced from a static context`. `greet` prints the field `greeting`. What is the fix that keeps the design sound?
hint: Does `greet` need an object's data?

choices.text: Make an object first, then call `greet()` on it
choices.why: Right: `greet` needs a greeting, so it needs the object that has one.

choices.text: Make `greet` static
choices.why: Then it cannot read `greeting` either, which then has to be static too, and soon everything is shared.

choices.text: Write `this.greet();` instead
choices.why: A static method has no `this`, so that fails for the same reason.

choices.text: Turn `main` into an instance method, as Java 21 allows
choices.why: Java 21 does not allow it: instance `main` methods come with Java 25's compact source files.

prompt: A field is declared `final List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>();`. Which line compiles?
hint: What exactly does `final` fix?

choices.text: `titles.clear();`
choices.why: Right: `final` fixes which list the field leads to, not what the list holds.

choices.text: `titles = new ArrayList<>();`
choices.why: That assigns the field a second time, which `final` refuses.

choices.text: `titles = null;`
choices.why: Also a second assignment; `null` is a value like any other.

prompt: `String branch = "Centro";` is read inside an anonymous class, and later in the method `branch = "Norte";` is added. The compiler now refuses the anonymous class. What problem is it preventing?
hint: What does the anonymous object keep: the variable, or its value?

choices.text: Two threads writing `branch` at once
choices.why: No thread is involved; the rule holds in a program with one.

choices.text: A `String` being changed, which strings do not allow
choices.why: The string never changes; `branch` would lead to a different string.

choices.text: The anonymous class outliving `main` and reading freed memory
choices.why: Java has no freed memory to read; the copy is exactly what lets the object outlive the method safely.

choices.text: A copy taken at creation drifting from the variable

prompt: Which of these does the compiler refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: `final` on a method, a class and a field each forbids one thing.

choices.text: `class MyString extends String { }`
choices.why: Yes: `String` is a final class, and no class may extend it.

choices.text: A subclass declaring its own version of a `final` method
choices.why: Yes: a final method cannot be overridden.

choices.text: A subclass calling a `final` method it inherited
choices.why: No: `final` stops a method being replaced, not being called.

choices.text: A constructor that ends without assigning a blank `final` field

prompt: A program hands thousands of small `Card` objects to a long-lived cache, and finds that every `Member` they came from also stays in memory. `Card` is declared inside `Member`. What is the likely cause, and the fix?

choices.text: `Card` is inner, its hidden field holds the member; make it `static`

prompt: A stack trace mentions the class `Sorting$1`. Nobody typed that name. What is it?

choices.text: A static nested class called `1` inside `Sorting`

prompt: A long-running program ends with `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. What is the first question to ask?
hint: The collector frees what nothing can reach.

choices.text: How to call `System.gc()` more often
choices.why: `System.gc()` is a request, and the collector already ran; it could free nothing that was still reachable.

choices.text: Which object's `finalize` failed to run
choices.why: Finalizers neither free memory reliably nor explain it; they are deprecated for removal.

choices.text: What still holds references it should have let go
choices.why: Right: everything still reachable stays, and a collection that only grows is the usual answer.

choices.text: How much more heap the JVM should be given with `-Xmx`
choices.why: That postpones the error when something keeps growing; it is a question for after the cause.

prompt: An object that no chain of references leads to from a root, such as a running method's local or a static field, is ___, and the collector may reuse its memory.
hint: The opposite of the word the lesson used for objects that stay.

prompt: `CountingSet extends HashSet` counts in an overridden `add` and also in an overridden `addAll`. Adding three ISBNs with `addAll` counts six. What is the sound fix?
hint: Whether `HashSet.addAll` calls `add` is not in its contract.

choices.text: Remove the count from `addAll`, since `HashSet` calls `add` anyway
choices.why: That works today and breaks the day `HashSet` stops calling `add`, with no edit to this class.

choices.text: Keep a `HashSet` in a private field and offer only the methods meant
choices.why: Right: composition depends on the set's public methods, not on how they happen to be written.

choices.text: Divide the count by two inside `addAll`
choices.why: That bakes the same hidden detail in twice; any change in `HashSet` breaks it again.

prompt: `Book extends Item`, and `Item` has `private int year`. Code inside `Book` writes `year = 2000;`. What happens?
hint: Lesson 14's rule, seen from a subclass.

choices.text: It compiles, because a subclass has every field of its superclass
choices.why: The book does have a year, set by `Item`'s constructor, and its own code still may not touch it.

choices.text: It compiles and creates a second `year` field in `Book`
choices.why: An assignment never declares a field; it would need a declaration to do that.

choices.text: It fails: `year has private access in Item`
choices.why: Right: `private` stops at the declaring class, subclasses included; `protected` or a method would open it.

choices.text: It fails until `Book` calls `super()` on its first line
choices.why: `super(...)` builds the item part; it grants no access to private fields.

prompt: An abstract class `Item` declares a constructor that takes a title. Since nobody can write `new Item(...)`, what is that constructor for?
hint: Who builds the `Item` part of a `Book`?

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses a constructor in an abstract class
choices.why: It accepts one; abstract only forbids `new` on the class itself.

choices.text: Subclasses call it with `super(title)`
choices.why: Right: every `Book` and `Dvd` runs it, so the shared field is set in one place.

choices.text: It runs once, when the class is loaded, to set up static fields
choices.why: That is a static block; a constructor runs for each object.

choices.text: Reflection uses it to create `Item` objects that `new` cannot
choices.why: Reflection is refused too: an abstract class has no instances of its own at all.

prompt: In a template method design, `Item.fee(days)` holds the algorithm and calls the abstract hook `dailyRate()`. Why mark `fee` itself `final`?
hint: What could a subclass do to `fee` otherwise?

choices.text: So that the JIT can inline it, which an abstract class needs
choices.why: Speed is not the reason the lesson gives, and the JIT inlines non-final methods as well.

choices.text: Because a method that calls an abstract method has to be final
choices.why: No such rule exists; the compiler would accept `fee` without `final`.

choices.text: So no subclass can replace the algorithm and skip its rules
choices.why: Right: subclasses fill in the hook; the steps around it, like the cap, stay the same for all.

prompt: `Shelf.getTitles()` returns its private `List<String>` field directly. What can a caller now do?
hint: `private` protects the field, not the object it points at.

choices.text: Add or remove titles in the shelf's own list
choices.why: Right: the caller holds the same list, so `private` stopped nothing.

choices.text: Only read it, since a getter returns a read-only copy
choices.why: A getter returns whatever its body returns; here, the list itself.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because the field is private
choices.why: The field is private; the list it refers to was handed out.

choices.text: Change the list only after casting it to `ArrayList`
choices.why: No cast is needed: `add` is on `List` already.

prompt: To return a list that the caller can read but that never changes and never follows later changes to the field, write `return List.___(titles);`.
hint: A copy, not a view.

prompt: Three classes each compute a late fee by calling `loan.getDaysLate()` and multiplying by 50. The rate changes to 75. What does tell-don't-ask say should have been done?
hint: Where does the number belong?

choices.text: A public constant `RATE` that the three classes all read
choices.why: That fixes the number and still leaves the rule copied three times.

choices.text: A method `loan.lateFee()`, so the rule lives in `Loan` once
choices.why: Right: callers ask for the answer, and the rule changes in one place.

choices.text: A setter `setRate` on each caller, so each can choose
choices.why: That multiplies the places where the rule can disagree with itself.

choices.text: Nothing: getters are the encapsulated way to share data
choices.why: A getter exposes a value; the rule that uses it still sits in three classes.

prompt: An interface used by ten classes gains a new method. When does adding it leave all ten compiling unchanged?
hint: Since Java 8 an interface method can have a body.

choices.text: When the new method is declared `abstract`
choices.why: An abstract method is exactly what each of the ten would then have to implement.

choices.text: Never: every implementer has to be recompiled with it
choices.why: Recompiling is not the problem; a missing implementation is, and a body removes it.

choices.text: When it is a `default` method with a body
choices.why: Right: classes that do not override it inherit the body.

prompt: `Book` extends `Item`, which has a public method `label()`, and implements `Lendable`, which has a default `label()` with the same signature. `Book` declares no `label()`. What happens?
hint: Two defaults clash; a class and a default do not.

choices.text: A compile error, as with two clashing defaults
choices.why: The error is for two interfaces; a superclass method takes part under a different rule.

choices.text: It compiles, and `Item.label()` runs: the class wins
choices.why: Right: a method inherited from a class beats a default method.

choices.text: It compiles, and the default runs, because the interface is named last
choices.why: Declaration order in `extends` and `implements` decides nothing.

choices.text: It compiles only if `Book` writes `Lendable.super.label()`
choices.why: That syntax chooses a default explicitly; here nothing needs choosing.

prompt: A class permitted by a sealed interface has to say one of three words. Match each to what it means.
hint: The hierarchy stops, stays closed, or opens.

pairs.right: It names its own permitted subclasses
Any class may extend it again

right_distractors: It may only be used inside its package

prompt: A class has `print(long n)` and `print(Integer n)`. Which one does `print(5)` call?
hint: Rank the conversions the compiler tries.

choices.text: `print(long)`
choices.why: Right: widening `int` to `long` is preferred to boxing it into `Integer`.

choices.text: `print(Integer)`, because `Integer` holds an `int` exactly
choices.why: Boxing is considered only if no widening match exists.

choices.text: Neither: the call is ambiguous and does not compile
choices.why: The ranking settles it, so there is no ambiguity here.

choices.text: Whichever is written first in the class
choices.why: Order in the source plays no part in choosing an overload.

prompt: When several overloads could take an argument, put the three ways the compiler can match it in the order it prefers them, best first.
hint: Varargs is the last resort.

prompt: `Book` declares `public boolean equals(Book other)` comparing ISBNs, and a correct `hashCode`. Two books with one ISBN go into a `HashSet`. What is its size, and why?
hint: Which `equals` does a collection call?

choices.text: 1, because the hash codes are equal and the set compares ISBNs
choices.why: The set calls `equals(Object)`, and `Book` never overrode that one.

choices.text: 1, because `HashSet` calls the most specific `equals` it finds
choices.why: Overloads are picked at compile time from the declared type, which inside the set is `Object`.

choices.text: 2: `equals(Book)` overloads `equals(Object)` and the set never calls it
choices.why: Right: `Object.equals` compares identity, and the two are different objects.

choices.text: It does not compile: `equals` must take `Object`
choices.why: It compiles; only `@Override` on it would have turned the mistake into an error.

prompt: `Item item = new Book(...);` and both classes declare `describe()`. Whose `describe()` runs on `item.describe()`?
hint: The object decides what runs.

choices.text: `Item`'s, because that is the variable's declared type
choices.why: The declared type decides what may be called; the object decides which body runs.

choices.text: `Book`'s
choices.why: Right: instance methods are bound dynamically, to the object's actual class.

choices.text: Both, `Item`'s first and then `Book`'s
choices.why: An override replaces; it runs `Item`'s only if it calls `super.describe()` itself.

prompt: `Item` and `Book` each declare a public field `name`, and `Book extends Item`. With `Item item = new Book();`, which `name` does `item.name` read?
hint: Fields do not take part in dynamic dispatch.

choices.text: `Item`'s, because a field is chosen by the declared type
choices.why: Right: `Book`'s field hides `Item`'s, and access is bound at compile time.

choices.text: `Book`'s, because the object is a `Book`
choices.why: That is how a method behaves; a field follows the variable's type.

choices.text: Neither: the compiler refuses two fields with one name
choices.why: It accepts it; the second field hides the first.

choices.text: Whichever constructor assigned last
choices.why: There are two separate fields in the object, and both keep their values.

prompt: Which of these are decided at compile time, by the declared type, rather than by the object at run time? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only overridable instance methods follow the object.

choices.text: Calling a `static` method through a variable
choices.why: Yes: static methods hide rather than override, and the declared type picks.

choices.text: Reading a field
choices.why: Yes: fields hide, and access goes by the declared type.

choices.text: Calling a public instance method a subclass overrides
choices.why: No: that is dynamic dispatch, decided by the object's class.

choices.text: Choosing between two overloads
choices.why: Yes: overload resolution happens in `javac`, from the argument's declared types.

choices.text: Calling an interface method on a variable of the interface's type
choices.why: No: the implementing object's method runs, chosen at run time.

prompt: A program writes `title.strip();` on a line of its own and then prints `title`, which still has its spaces. Why?
hint: What does a method on an immutable object give back?

choices.text: `strip` only removes tabs, not spaces
choices.why: It removes both; the result was simply not kept.

choices.text: Strings are cached, so the print showed an older copy
choices.why: There is one string and it was never changed; caching plays no part.

choices.text: `strip` returned a new string, and the line threw it away
choices.why: Right: `title = title.strip();` keeps it.

prompt: In a builder for an immutable `Loan`, where are the rules about the parts, such as a due date after the start date, checked?
hint: Only one method sees every part at once.

choices.text: In each `withX` setter, as the value arrives
choices.why: A setter sees one part; a rule between two parts cannot be checked until both are in.

choices.text: In `build()`, once, with every part in view
choices.why: Right: `build()` validates and then creates the loan.

choices.text: In the caller, before the builder is created
choices.why: Then every caller repeats the rules, and one of them will forget.

choices.text: Nowhere: a builder's purpose is to skip validation
choices.why: Its purpose is a readable way to pass many parts; validation stays.

prompt: `Book extends Item`, and neither class has been used yet. Put these steps of the first `new Book()` in the order they run.
hint: The superclass first, at both levels.

prompt: A program creates five `Book` objects. How many times does `Book`'s static block run?
hint: It belongs to the class, not to an object.

prompt: `Item`'s constructor calls `describe()`, which `Book` overrides to print its field `pages`, declared `int pages = 100;`. What does the first line printed by `new Book()` show for `pages`?
hint: Whose part of the object is built first?

choices.text: 100, because the initialiser is on the same line as the field
choices.why: The initialiser runs in step 5, after `Item`'s constructor has already made the call.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses an overridable call in a constructor
choices.why: It compiles without a word; that is why it is a trap.

choices.text: `Item`'s version runs instead, since `Book` is not built yet
choices.why: Dispatch follows the object's class from the start: `Book`'s version runs.

choices.text: 0: `Book`'s initialisers have not run yet
choices.why: Right: the override runs on an object whose `Book` part still holds defaults.

prompt: A file saves each book's genre as `genre.ordinal()`. A new constant is inserted at the top of the enum. What happens to the saved books when they are read back?
hint: What does an ordinal measure?

choices.text: They read back correctly, since an ordinal is fixed when a constant is created
choices.why: An ordinal is the position in the list, and every position after the insert moved.

choices.text: Reading fails with an exception for every book
choices.why: Nothing fails: each number still names some constant, just the wrong one.

choices.text: Every book comes back one genre off, with no error
choices.why: Right: store `name()` instead, which survives an insert.

prompt: To turn the text `"POETRY"` back into the constant `Genre.POETRY`, call `Genre.___("POETRY")`.
hint: It throws if the name is not exact.

prompt: Given `record Isbn(String value) {}`, how do you read the component from an `Isbn` called `isbn`?
hint: Accessors are named after the components.

choices.text: `isbn.getValue()`
choices.why: Records do not follow the `get` convention.

choices.text: `isbn.value`, since the field is public
choices.why: The field is `private final`; the accessor is the way in.

choices.text: `isbn.get("value")`
choices.why: There is no lookup by name; each component has its own method.

choices.text: `isbn.value()`
choices.why: Right: one accessor per component, with the component's name.

prompt: `record Shelf(String name, List<String> titles) {}` is built from an `ArrayList`. Later the code that built it adds a title to that `ArrayList`. Does the shelf change?
hint: A record is as immutable as its components.

choices.text: Yes, unless the compact constructor stores `List.copyOf(titles)`
choices.why: Right: the final field holds the same list; a copy in the constructor cuts the link.

choices.text: No, because a record copies every component it is given
choices.why: A record stores what it is given; copying is the author's job.

choices.text: No, because the field is `final`
choices.why: `final` fixes the reference, not the contents of the list it points at.

choices.text: It throws, because records forbid mutable components
choices.why: Records accept any component type; nothing checks mutability.

prompt: `int a = 3, b = 5;` and `swap(a, b)` exchanges its two parameters inside the method. What does `System.out.println(a)` print afterwards?
hint: The method got copies.

prompt: A method `void reset(Book b) { b = new Book("blank"); }` is called as `reset(mine)`. What happens to `mine`?
hint: Two arrows, then one of them moves.

choices.text: `mine` now refers to the blank book
choices.why: Only the copy of the reference, `b`, was pointed at the new book.

choices.text: The original book's fields are overwritten with the blank one's
choices.why: Assigning to `b` moves an arrow; it copies no fields into any object.

choices.text: It does not compile: a parameter cannot be reassigned
choices.why: It compiles; a parameter is a local variable unless declared `final`.

choices.text: Nothing: `mine` still refers to the same book, unchanged
choices.why: Right: Java passed a copy of the reference, and reassigning a copy reaches nobody.

prompt: `List<Integer> ids` holds `[7, 3, 5]`. After `ids.remove(2)`, what does it hold?
hint: An `int` literal and two methods called `remove`.

choices.text: `[7, 3, 5]`, because no element equals 2
choices.why: That would be `remove(Object)`; given an `int`, the compiler picks `remove(int index)`.
Right: `2` is an index here, and index 2 holds the 5.

choices.text: `[3, 5]`, because the first element is removed
choices.why: Removing index 0 would do that; the argument was 2.

choices.text: A compile error, because the call is ambiguous
choices.why: It is not ambiguous: the `int` version matches without boxing, so it wins.

prompt: A method receives `List<String> titles` and calls `titles.add("Emma")`. One caller passes `Arrays.asList(shelf)`, another `List.of("Dune")`. What happens?
hint: Neither of those two builds a list that can grow.

choices.text: The first works, because it copies the array into a new list
choices.why: `Arrays.asList` wraps the array without copying it, and an array cannot grow.

choices.text: Both throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, every time
choices.why: Right: one is a fixed-size view of an array, the other cannot change at all, and the `List` type hides both facts.

choices.text: Neither compiles, because those methods do not return a `List`
choices.why: Both return `List`, which is exactly why the compiler cannot warn.

choices.text: The second works, since `List.of` only refuses `set`
choices.why: `List.of` refuses every change, size and elements alike.

prompt: An `ArrayList` grows its inner array from 10 slots to 15, then 22. Following the same rule, how many slots does the array that replaces a full 22 have?
hint: The old length plus half of it, rounded down.

prompt: A program must answer, thousands of times a second, whether an ISBN has already been seen. Which collection fits?
hint: "Is this one in there?"

choices.text: An `ArrayList` searched with `contains`
choices.why: `contains` on a list reads elements one by one until it finds a match: a `Set` written the slow way.

choices.text: A `HashSet`
choices.why: Right: the hash code jumps to a bucket, and the question is exactly the one a `Set` is built for.

choices.text: A `TreeMap` from ISBN to `true`
choices.why: A map with a dummy value is a set in disguise, and the sorted order is paid for and never read.

choices.text: A `LinkedList`, because no element is read by position
choices.why: A linked list still walks node by node to answer `contains`.

prompt: A `Book` class overrides `equals` by ISBN and not `hashCode`. Two equal books go into a `HashSet`. What does the set report?
hint: Which step of a hash lookup decides the bucket?

choices.text: Size 1, because `equals` stops the second one
choices.why: `equals` is only compared inside a bucket, and the two books landed in different ones.

choices.text: An exception on the second `add`, naming the broken contract
choices.why: Nothing checks the contract: the set is wrong, silently.

choices.text: Size 2, and `contains` of a third equal book is false
choices.why: Right: `Object`'s `hashCode` gives each object its own number, so equal books never meet.

prompt: Match each `Map` class to the order it iterates its keys in.
hint: They mirror the three sets.

pairs.right: The order keys were first inserted

right_distractors: The order values were last changed

prompt: A help desk takes requests in arrival order, and an empty desk at night is normal. Which pair of declaration and call reads best?
hint: Throwing form for a mistake, special value for a normal outcome.

choices.text: `Queue<Request> q = new ArrayDeque<>()` and `q.poll()`, testing for `null`
choices.why: Right: first in, first out, and `poll` answers `null` for the normal empty case.

choices.text: `Stack<Request>` and `pop()`
choices.why: A stack serves the newest request first, and `pop` throws on empty.

choices.text: `Queue<Request> q = new LinkedList<>()` and `q.remove()`
choices.why: `remove()` throws on an empty queue, and `LinkedList` is the slower queue.

choices.text: `PriorityQueue<Request>` and `peek()`
choices.why: A priority queue serves the smallest, not the earliest, and `peek` never takes anything out.

prompt: Why does the JDK's own documentation steer you from `Stack` to `Deque` for a stack?
hint: What does `Stack` extend?

choices.text: `Stack` cannot hold more than 1024 elements
choices.why: There is no such limit; the problem is what `Stack` lets you do, not how much it holds.

choices.text: It extends `Vector`, so list methods such as `add(0, x)` and `get(i)` reach past the top, and every call pays for locking
choices.why: Right: it is-a list in the code and not in meaning, and its methods are `synchronized`.

choices.text: `Stack.pop` returns `null` on an empty stack, hiding mistakes
choices.why: `pop` throws on empty, as the deque's does; the problem lies elsewhere.

prompt: A `for-each` over an `ArrayList` calls `loans.remove(loan)` on a match, and the program finishes without an exception. What can you conclude?
hint: When does the iterator check `modCount`?

choices.text: That removing inside a `for-each` is safe for this list
choices.why: It is never safe: the check is best-effort, `hasNext` does not make it, and the next run can fail.

choices.text: That the JVM can copy the list for the loop
choices.why: No copy is made: the loop walks the list itself through its iterator.

choices.text: Nothing: the check that throws simply did not run
choices.why: Right: if the removal leaves the cursor at the size, `hasNext` says done and the check never runs.

choices.text: That the matching element was the first one
choices.why: The position that slips through is the one next to the end, not the first.

prompt: To remove from a list every element that matches a condition, without writing a loop, call `list.___(...)`.
hint: The shortest of the four safe ways.

prompt: Which of these change a list safely while it is being walked? Choose all that apply.
hint: Whatever changes the list must be whatever walks it.

choices.text: `it.remove()` on an explicit `Iterator`
choices.why: Yes: the iterator makes the change itself and keeps its count in step.

choices.text: `list.add(x)` inside a `for-each` over the same list
choices.why: No: the change comes from outside the iterator, a structural one.

choices.text: `ListIterator.set` and `ListIterator.add`
choices.why: Yes: the list iterator made each insertion, so it walks past them cleanly.

choices.text: A `for-each` over `List.copyOf(list)` that removes from `list`
choices.why: Yes: the walk is over a copy that does not change.

prompt: A method `double total(List<Number> amounts)` refuses a `List<Integer>`. Which signature accepts it and still lets the method read the values?
hint: Producer `extends`, consumer `super`.

choices.text: `double total(List<? extends Number> amounts)`
choices.why: Right: the method only reads, so the list is a producer of `Number`s.

choices.text: `double total(List<? super Number> amounts)`, so that any list of numbers fits
choices.why: `? super Number` accepts lists of `Number` or `Object`, not `Integer`.

choices.text: `double total(List amounts)`, the raw type
choices.why: It compiles with warnings and gives up the check the brackets were for.

choices.text: No signature: generics forbid passing a subtype's list
choices.why: A wildcard is the way to say a method accepts lists of subtypes.

prompt: A raw `List` collects titles, and somebody adds an `Integer` by mistake. Where does the program fail, and why is that a problem?
hint: The cast is where the damage is found.

choices.text: At the `add`, which throws `ClassCastException` immediately
choices.why: A raw list accepts anything; nothing is checked at the `add`.

choices.text: At compile time, because `javac` refuses raw types
choices.why: `javac` compiles raw types with an unchecked note; it does not refuse them.

choices.text: Later, at a cast far from the `add`, so the stack trace points away from the mistake
choices.why: Right: the trace names where the value was read, in a real program another class, written by another person.

prompt: Because of type ___, a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are the same class at run time.
hint: The compiler removes the type arguments.

prompt: A stack trace is printed for an exception thrown in `daysLate`, called by `fine`, called by `main`. Put its lines in the order they are printed.
hint: The most recent call first.

prompt: Why must a caller of `Files.readString` catch or declare `IOException`, when a caller of `Integer.parseInt` need not catch anything?
hint: It depends on the exception's class.

choices.text: `readString` can fail, and `parseInt` succeeds on any string
choices.why: `parseInt` fails readily, with `NumberFormatException`.

choices.text: `IOException` is checked; `NumberFormatException` extends `RuntimeException`
choices.why: Right: a missing file meets a correct program, a bad number is a bug, and the classes say so.

choices.text: File access is a privileged operation the compiler audits
choices.why: The compiler knows nothing about files; it reads the `throws` clause of the method called.

choices.text: `parseInt` catches its own exception internally
choices.why: It throws it to the caller, which is why the program ended with a stack trace.

prompt: A method's `try` throws an exception, and its `finally` contains `return "ok";`. What does the caller see?
hint: What leaves the method when `finally` returns?

choices.text: The exception, because `finally` leaves what is thrown alone
choices.why: A `return` in `finally` replaces whatever was leaving, an exception included.

choices.text: `"ok"`, and the exception is gone without a trace
choices.why: Right: no stack trace, no message, which is why the compiler warns with `-Xlint:finally`.

choices.text: A compile error, since a `finally` may not contain `return`
choices.why: It compiles; only a lint warning flags it.

choices.text: Both, as a suppressed exception attached to the result
choices.why: Suppressed exceptions belong to try-with-resources and ride on an exception, never on a return value.

prompt: `try (var a = open("a"); var b = open("b")) { ... } catch (Exception e) { ... } finally { ... }` and the body throws. Put what happens in order.
hint: Reverse order to close, and everything closed before the handler.

prompt: In a try-with-resources, the body throws and then `close` throws too. What does the caller receive?
hint: Which of the two explains why the work did not happen?

choices.text: The exception from `close`, which replaced the first
choices.why: That is the masking a hand-written `finally` causes; try-with-resources keeps the first.

choices.text: A new exception wrapping both as causes
choices.why: No new exception is made, and a cause is a different relation.

choices.text: The body's, with the `close` failure as suppressed
choices.why: Right: the `Suppressed:` line sits under the body's own trace.

prompt: A server loop wraps each request in `catch (Exception e)` and logs the error. A request recurses without end. What does the `catch` do?
hint: Where does `StackOverflowError` sit in the tree?

choices.text: It logs the error and the loop carries on
choices.why: `StackOverflowError` is not an `Exception`, so this `catch` does not match it.

choices.text: Nothing: `StackOverflowError` is an `Error` and passes it
choices.why: Right: it descends from `Error`, the other branch under `Throwable`.

choices.text: It catches it only if the method declares `throws StackOverflowError`
choices.why: Declaring an unchecked throwable changes nothing about which `catch` matches.

prompt: A loader catches an `IOException` it cannot handle and throws `new CatalogueException("cannot load the catalogue")`. What is lost, and how is it kept?
hint: The JDK's report of what actually went wrong.

choices.text: The original exception and its trace; pass it as the cause, so `Caused by:` prints it
choices.why: Right: the new exception says what failed here, and the cause says why.

choices.text: No information, because the message already says what went wrong
choices.why: It says what failed in this program and not why: the missing file is gone.

choices.text: The line number; add it to the message by hand
choices.why: The new exception has its own trace; what goes is the original's.

choices.text: The checked status; make `CatalogueException` extend `IOException`
choices.why: Checked or not is a separate decision; the lost information is the original exception.

prompt: A framework finds methods marked `@Check` by reflection while the program runs. Which retention must `@Check` declare?
hint: Only one of the three reaches the running program.

choices.text: `CLASS`, the default
choices.why: `CLASS` writes it into the class file and the JVM does not load it.

choices.text: `SOURCE`
choices.why: The compiler drops it after compiling, so nothing at run time could see it.

choices.text: `RUNTIME`
choices.why: Right: only a `RUNTIME` annotation is visible to reflection.

prompt: A class declares `public String tostring()` with `@Override` above it. What happens?
hint: What does `@Override` ask the compiler to check?

choices.text: It compiles, and printing the object uses the new method
choices.why: The lowercase `s` makes it a different method; nothing would call it.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: nothing above has that method
choices.why: Right: the annotation turns the typo into a compile error.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning, and `toString` is renamed
choices.why: The compiler renames nothing; it refuses the file.

choices.text: It fails at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`
choices.why: The check happens at compile time, before anything runs.

prompt: A library's `module-info.java` exports `com.example.library.api` and not `com.example.library.internal`. An app module imports a `public` class from `internal`. What happens?
hint: To the app module, what is that package?

choices.text: It compiles, because the class is `public`
choices.why: Above the package, the module decides; `public` is no longer enough.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning and fails when run
choices.why: The refusal comes at compile time.

choices.text: `javac` answers as if the package did not exist
choices.why: Right: an unexported package is not part of what the library offers.

prompt: A typical application, built with Maven and a web framework, has no `module-info.java`. Where does it run?
hint: Lesson 18's project, and nearly every service.

choices.text: On the class path, as nearly all Java software does
choices.why: Right: modules bind only code that runs as modules.

choices.text: It cannot run on Java 25 without a module declaration
choices.why: Class-path applications run on every release since 9.

choices.text: On the module path, where `java` turns it into a module
choices.why: That would make it an automatic or named module; a plain application stays on the class path.

choices.text: Inside a runtime built with `jlink`
choices.why: `jlink` refuses a program that is not modular.
